title: Database Indexing
summary: Use query plans and selective predicates to choose indexes, because each faster lookup adds storage and write work.
body:
An index is an auxiliary structure for finding rows without reading the whole table. It is not a blanket “make queries fast” switch: an index that does not match the filter or sort can sit unused while adding work to every write.

## Why B-trees work

PostgreSQL's default B-tree index stores sorted keys in pages, with internal pages directing searches to leaves and leaves identifying matching rows. This supports equality and ordered ranges: an index on created_at can find yesterday's rows or scan recent rows in order. The work is roughly logarithmic in index entries plus the rows fetched, but the actual cost depends on selectivity and I/O. An index on a low-cardinality boolean like is_active may be ignored if half the table qualifies; scanning the table can be cheaper than following many index pointers.

B-trees are not a full-text search engine. For searching words within documents use an inverted index, such as PostgreSQL's GIN index over a tsvector or Elasticsearch, rather than expecting a normal B-tree on body text to help with arbitrary words.

## Composite order matters

| Index | Query pattern it can efficiently support | Poor fit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| (tenant_id, created_at) | WHERE tenant_id = ?; same filter with date range or date sort | WHERE created_at = ? alone |
| (status, created_at) | WHERE status = ? ORDER BY created_at | WHERE created_at = ? alone |

This is the leftmost-prefix rule: the keys of a composite B-tree are ordered first by its first column, then by the second within each first-column value. A query on B alone cannot generally seek into (A, B) as if B were the leading key. There are engine-specific exceptions and planner strategies, so verify with EXPLAIN rather than treating the rule as a syntax ban. Put equality predicates that match common access paths first, then useful range/sort columns; cardinality and query frequency matter more than the slogan “most selective first.”

## Cover the query, not every table

A covering index contains the fields needed for one query, allowing an index-only scan when visibility and engine conditions permit. For a query selecting id and created_at for a tenant, a suitable index with those values may avoid fetching the full table row. Covering does not mean indexing all database tables, and wider indexes consume more RAM and disk. Check the execution plan: a narrow SELECT may benefit while SELECT * does not.

Every INSERT adds index entries; UPDATE or DELETE may also modify them, causing extra I/O, page splits or contention. Ten indexes on a write-heavy events table can cost more than one slow occasional report. Remove redundant indexes, consider a partial index for a selective common condition, and benchmark with representative data. An index does not fix an N+1 query or an unnecessarily large result set.

## How to answer this in an interview

> For 10 million orders, if users request their latest 20 orders, I would add a B-tree on (user_id, created_at DESC), check EXPLAIN on realistic data, and consider including only the returned columns for an index-only scan. I would not add a standalone status index until its selectivity and read savings outweigh the write tax.
keyTakeaways: B-trees support equality and range access; full-text search needs an inverted index.
The leftmost prefix determines which composite index lookups are efficient.
Covering indexes serve a specific query from index entries, subject to engine visibility rules.
Each index costs storage and write throughput; use realistic plans and cardinality to justify it.
